summary: Addresses how to protect the integrity of data in a routing policy system. It provides an authentication and authorization model so that only the right parties can change routing policy information. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC sets rules for changing routing registry records. It checks both the identity of the person making a change and whether that person has permission for the specific record.

questions: how is routing policy data secured
subtitle: Rules for proving who may change routing policy data and which changes they may make.

tldr.problem: Routing registries are used to support network operations, but weak controls can let unauthorized or mistaken data changes affect routing decisions.
tldr.mechanism: Maintainer objects define authentication, while authorization follows relationships among AS, address and route objects. Route additions require approval for both the origin AS and address prefix.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines change authorization for routing registry data; query authorization and a fully distributed registry are out of scope. RFC 4012 later updates it.

facts.label: RIPE schema described

today: RFC 2725 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4012; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Routing Registries Need Integrity
sections.content:
A routing registry stores information about routing policy. The RFC explains that such data began as advice for debugging but was increasingly used for operational purposes. Incorrect or unauthorized entries could therefore undermine the integrity of routing information.

Internet routing protocols do not prove that a route announcement is legitimate. A more specific prefix can take precedence over a broader route, so a false specific route may disrupt access. This document addresses delegated authority and data integrity; distributed-registry design is left to other work.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing registries can influence how networks treat route announcements. The RFC adds controls because an incorrect entry could affect traffic beyond the person who entered it.

sections.title: Assumptions and Scope
sections.content:
The authorization model assumes that address space is allocated in levels and that AS numbers are allocated singly or in blocks. It also assumes that a route should be announced with consent from both the origin AS holder and the address-space holder. Registries may choose weaker rules for selected parts of their data.

The RFC covers authentication and authorization for adding, changing and deleting records. It does not define authorization for database queries, mutual authentication of queries, transaction formats or a complete distributed registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The model follows delegated ownership: larger allocations can be assigned to smaller holders. It controls who may change records, not who may read them.

sections.title: Authentication with Maintainers
sections.content:
A maintainer object stores the authentication checks for a group of records. Other objects refer to maintainers, commonly through mnt-by. The RFC describes mail-header matching and encrypted-password methods as weak, and describes PGP-based signatures as stronger options; repositories may reject weak methods.

The method is separate from authorization. Authentication establishes who submitted a transaction; authorization decides whether that identity may make the requested change. The RFC also permits multiple signatures so repositories that support different techniques can verify a transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication answers who is making a change. Authorization answers whether that person may change this particular record.

sections.title: Delegation and Maintainer Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC makes mnt-by mandatory and adds the as-block object to record delegated ranges of AS numbers. Attributes such as mnt-routes and mnt-lower let a holder authorize maintainers to add more specific route or allocation records.

reclaim can let a less-specific object retain rights to modify or delete subordinate objects, while no-reclaim can exclude selected objects. Maintainer referral information records who created a maintainer; an auth-override can support recovery when a maintainer has been inactive for the specified period.
sections.plainLanguage: Maintainers can delegate limited permission for smaller pieces of address or route space. A covering record may also retain carefully limited recovery rights over records below it.

sections.title: Checking Additions and Changes
sections.content:
A new route object must pass authorization checks for its origin AS and its address prefix. The registry first checks an exact route match, then the longest less-specific route, and then an allocated address record when no route match applies. If the AS record does not exist, the route addition is rejected.

Changing or deleting an existing object requires authorization from its maintainer or an applicable reclaim rule. A deletion is treated as a special kind of modification and may leave a record marked as deleted.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding a route needs permission from both the AS side and the address side. Changing or deleting an existing record needs permission from its maintainer or an applicable recovery rule.

sections.title: Deployment and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says registry use and strict prefix filtering were not universal at the time. Existing data could be stale, lack maintainers or have weak authentication. It suggests a staged transition that strengthens authorization, adds delegation support, improves registry cooperation and eventually removes clearly unused data.

Mirrors can independently check transactions only if they have complete data and process changes in order. Authentication and authorization of queries remain outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Older registry records may be incomplete or outdated, so stronger rules need a gradual transition. A mirror can check changes only when it has the complete history in order.
